newsitem.title: USA: U.S. markets to watch for rate hint from Greenspan.
newsitem.headline: U.S. markets to watch for rate hint from Greenspan.

text.p: U.S. financial markets will zero in on hints from Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan this week regarding the odds and timing of an interest rate move in 1997, market players said.
"The one thing people will be looking for is what he wants to do with rates," one strategist at a primary dealer said.
Greenspan is set to deliver his Humphrey-Hawkins testimony before the Senate Banking Committee on Wednesday. His testimony before the House Banking Committee has been rescheduled for March 5.
"We already pretty much know what he will say about the economy," the strategist said, referring to Greenspan's January 21 testimony before the Senate Budget Committee.
-- The economy "has retained considerable vigor with few signs of the imbalances and inflationary tensions that have disrupted past expansions."

-- The unemployment rate edged down to the low 5.0-percent readings, "roughly matching the low of the last cyclical upswing in the late 1980s," but without "a broad increase in inflation," a development which he tied to job insecurity.
A source close to the Fed told Reuters that Greenspan had already given hints about the future direction of interest rates in that testimony, when he said:

-- "The trade-off of subdued growth for job security has to come to an end," a point Greenspan already made in his February 1996 testimony, and that it is a "transitional phenomenon.... (that) may already be running its course."

The source pointed out the presence of a tightening bias since July 1996, introduced as the unemployment rate was edging down to 5.5 percent, "did not indicate an imminent move but the likelihood of the direction of the next move."

The December 17, 1996 Federal Open Market Committee minutes, the latest available, showed policy makers "did view the next policy move as more likely to be in the direction of some firming than toward easing."
One Fed source noted that after posting its best year-over-year performance in three decades, the core Consumer Price Index was bound to edge up in 1997.

"It's likely to be similar or a little higher this year," the source said, stressing that any anticipatory Fed move to quell budding inflation would be limited in scope. "We are not looking at the same situation as in 1994."

While the wage component of the Employment Cost Index -- a much-watched indicator by Greenspan's admission -- accelerated since the unemployment rate dipped through 5.5 percent in mid-1996, there is no sign of commodity inflation.
The year-over-year core crude and core intermediate components of the Producer Price Index that rose in double digits in 1994 are now posting negative readings.
The source noted that Greenspan stressed on January 21 "the last thing we want to do is to inhibit economic growth to try to fine-tune the various different aspects of labor markets and other areas."

The source said Fed officials view the 5.25-percent funds rate as close to its appropriate level and that, although, current economic conditions may warrant a "somewhat tighter policy" Greenspan "said we are not in the business of fine-tuning the economy."

Greenspan, however, last month reiterated the need for a preemptive policy move when he said "it is not the conditions prevailing today that are critical but rather those likely to prevail six to 12 months" from now.

The Fed chairman must testify on the economy and monetary policy twice a year under the 1978 Full Employment and Balanced Growth Act that governs the U.S. central bank. The testimonies include the Fed's economic forecasts for the year.
